questions.question_text: A bowed-outward production possibilities curve reflects:
questions.option_b: increasing opportunity costs as resources are not equally suited to all goods
questions.explanation: The outward bow shows that shifting resources costs more and more of the other good, because resources aren't perfectly adaptable. A straight-line PPC would mean constant opportunity costs.

questions.question_text: The 'invisible hand' refers to the idea that:
questions.option_b: individuals pursuing self-interest can unintentionally promote society's good through markets
questions.option_c: prices are set by central planners
questions.explanation: Adam Smith's metaphor: market prices coordinate self-interested decisions into efficient outcomes without central direction. It's the case for decentralized markets, the opposite of central planning.

questions.question_text: A normative economic statement is:
questions.option_b: 'The government should raise the minimum wage.'
questions.explanation: Normative = value judgment ('should'); positive = factual/testable. The other three describe what IS, not what OUGHT to be. The 'should' is the giveaway.

questions.question_text: The CPI measures:
questions.option_b: the average price change of a fixed basket of consumer goods over time
questions.explanation: The Consumer Price Index tracks the cost of a fixed market basket, the main gauge of inflation faced by households. GDP measures output; the deflator is a broader price index.

questions.question_text: Which is counted in the labor force?
questions.option_a: a full-time college student not seeking work
questions.option_b: a retired person
questions.option_c: an unemployed person actively searching for a job
questions.explanation: Labor force = employed + unemployed actively seeking work. Students, retirees, and discouraged workers are OUT of the labor force, which is why discouraged workers leaving lowers the measured unemployment rate.

questions.question_text: Real GDP is preferred to nominal GDP for comparing output across years because it:
questions.option_b: adjusts for inflation, isolating changes in actual production
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP rises with both higher prices and more output; real GDP holds prices constant (base year) to show true production change. Comparing welfare across years requires the inflation adjustment.

questions.question_text: If the CPI rises from 200 to 220, the inflation rate over that period is:
questions.explanation: Inflation = (new − old)/old = (220 − 200)/200 = 0.10 = 10%. Using the raw difference (20) as a percent, or dividing by 100, are the common errors.

questions.question_text: The aggregate demand curve slopes downward partly because of the:
questions.option_a: wealth effect — lower price levels raise real purchasing power
questions.option_b: law of diminishing returns
questions.explanation: Lower price levels increase real wealth, real money balances (interest-rate effect), and net exports — all raising quantity of AD demanded. These are different from the microeconomic reasons a single demand curve slopes down.

questions.question_text: An increase in consumer confidence would shift:
questions.option_b: aggregate demand right
questions.explanation: Optimistic consumers spend more, raising consumption (a component of AD) → AD shifts right. Confidence affects demand, not productive capacity (LRAS) or short-run costs (SRAS).

questions.question_text: In an inflationary gap, the appropriate contractionary fiscal policy is:
questions.option_b: decrease government spending or raise taxes
questions.explanation: An inflationary gap (output above potential) calls for reducing AD: cut spending or raise taxes. Options C and D are EXPANSIONARY monetary tools — wrong direction and wrong policy type.

questions.question_text: The MPC + MPS always equals:
questions.explanation: Every additional dollar of income is either spent (MPC) or saved (MPS), so MPC + MPS = 1. The spending multiplier is 1/MPS = 1/(1−MPC) — related but not equal to the sum.

questions.question_text: Which is the most liquid component of the money supply (M1)?
questions.option_b: currency and checkable deposits
questions.explanation: M1 is the narrowest, most liquid measure: cash and checking deposits usable immediately. CDs and bonds (less liquid) sit in broader measures; real estate isn't money at all.

questions.question_text: In the money market, an increase in the money supply causes the nominal interest rate to:
questions.option_b: fall
questions.explanation: More money supplied (vertical MS shifts right) along a downward-sloping money demand curve lowers the equilibrium nominal interest rate. This is the channel by which the Fed stimulates borrowing.

questions.question_text: Bond prices and interest rates have what relationship?
questions.option_a: they move in the same direction
questions.option_b: they move in opposite directions
questions.explanation: When rates rise, existing bonds paying lower fixed coupons become less attractive, so their prices fall — an inverse relationship. This underlies how open-market operations move rates.

questions.question_text: If the Fed wants to RAISE interest rates, it should:
questions.option_a: buy bonds and lower the reserve requirement
questions.option_b: sell bonds, draining reserves from the banking system
questions.explanation: Selling bonds pulls reserves out of banks → less lending → money supply contracts → rates rise. Buying bonds, cutting the reserve requirement, and lowering the discount rate are all expansionary.

questions.question_text: The short-run Phillips curve illustrates a trade-off between:
questions.option_b: GDP and the money supply
questions.explanation: Higher inflation is associated with lower unemployment in the short run (and vice versa) as demand changes. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate, breaking the trade-off.

questions.question_text: Expansionary monetary policy in the long run, per the AD-AS model, primarily raises:
questions.option_b: the price level, with real GDP returning to potential
questions.explanation: In the long run the SRAS adjusts and output returns to potential (LRAS), leaving only a higher price level — money neutrality. Short-run gains in real GDP are temporary.

questions.question_text: Economic growth in the AD-AS model is best shown by:
questions.option_a: a rightward shift of aggregate demand
questions.option_b: a rightward shift of the long-run aggregate supply curve
questions.explanation: Long-run growth = expanded productive capacity = LRAS shifts right (more resources, better technology). AD shifts change output in the short run but not the economy's potential.

questions.question_text: In the foreign exchange market, increased demand for a country's exports will:
questions.option_b: appreciate its currency
questions.option_c: have no effect on the currency
questions.explanation: Foreign buyers need the country's currency to pay for exports → demand for the currency rises → it appreciates. Export demand and currency demand move together.

questions.question_text: A depreciation of the U.S. dollar will tend to:
questions.option_a: make U.S. exports more expensive abroad
questions.option_b: make U.S. exports cheaper abroad and imports more expensive
questions.explanation: A weaker dollar means foreigners pay less for U.S. goods (exports up) while Americans pay more for foreign goods (imports down) — typically improving the trade balance.

questions.question_text: Expansionary fiscal policy that raises U.S. interest rates can REDUCE net exports because:
questions.option_b: higher rates attract foreign capital, appreciating the dollar and making exports pricier
questions.option_d: it has no effect on exchange rates
questions.explanation: Higher rates draw foreign investment → dollar appreciates → exports fall. This 'net export effect' is a second channel (alongside crowding out) that offsets fiscal stimulus in an open economy.

questions.question_text: A nation has comparative advantage in a good when it can produce that good at a:
questions.option_a: higher opportunity cost than trading partners
questions.option_b: lower opportunity cost than trading partners
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage rests on LOWER opportunity cost — what you give up to produce the good. Absolute advantage (raw quantity) doesn't determine the gains from trade; relative cost does.

questions.question_text: Marginal analysis says a rational actor takes an action when:
questions.option_b: marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
questions.explanation: Decisions are made at the margin: do it as long as the extra benefit of one more unit exceeds the extra cost. Total benefit being positive doesn't mean the LAST unit was worth its cost.

questions.question_text: Which phase of the business cycle is characterized by falling output and rising unemployment?
questions.option_b: peak
questions.explanation: A recession is the contraction phase: real GDP falls and unemployment climbs. The peak is the top before the downturn; expansion and recovery are upturns.

questions.question_text: Cost-push inflation originates from:
questions.option_b: a leftward shift of short-run aggregate supply (e.g., higher input costs)
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation comes from the supply side — higher production costs shift SRAS left, raising prices and lowering output. Demand-pull inflation, by contrast, comes from rising AD.

questions.question_text: Fractional reserve banking means banks:
questions.option_b: keep only a fraction of deposits in reserve and lend out the rest
questions.explanation: Banks hold a fraction (the required reserve ratio) and lend the rest, which is how the money multiplier expands the money supply. Holding 100% would eliminate money creation through lending.

questions.question_text: Stagflation poses a policy dilemma because:
questions.option_a: inflation and unemployment can be fixed simultaneously
questions.option_b: policies that fight inflation worsen unemployment, and vice versa
questions.explanation: Stagflation (high inflation + high unemployment from a supply shock) means demand-side tools can only address one problem by worsening the other — there's no easy AD fix, unlike a simple demand shock.

questions.question_text: A tariff is:
questions.option_b: a subsidy to exporters
questions.option_c: a limit on the money supply
questions.explanation: A tariff taxes imports, raising their price to protect domestic producers — but it reduces trade gains and raises consumer prices. A quota limits quantity; a subsidy supports producers.

questions.question_text: Nominal interest rate minus inflation equals the:
questions.option_b: real interest rate
questions.explanation: The Fisher equation: real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation. It's the true cost of borrowing after stripping out inflation — what matters for saving and investment decisions.
